video_title: A Bear Market Inside a Bull Market
gist: Jordi Visser argues higher rates and oil are not a repeat of past disasters because credit spreads, jobless claims and margins show no stress, calling this a bear market inside a bull market where small caps and rate-sensitive sectors suffer while AI infrastructure and Mag 7 lead. His main new thesis is that consumer agents (Meta's Muse) and tokenization make crypto the next big trade.

themes.theme: Rates are not the threat: fact-based checks

insights.claim: Visser argues that the fear that rising rates cause disasters is a linear, backtest-based story from a pre-AI, pre-tokenization era, and lists indicators that would change his mind: S&P year-over-year turning negative, widening credit spreads and rising jobless claims.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Gives concrete tripwires instead of narratives for a rate-driven equity selloff.
insights.quote: If year-over-year S&P goes negative, I'll change my mind

insights.claim: Visser says none of the recession or contagion signals are present: the leading economic index just turned positive without a recession, Moody's BA-to-10-year credit spreads are not widening, jobless claims are not budging, profit margins are still rising, and S&P is up about 17% year-over-year.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Supports staying constructive on equities despite higher yields.

insights.claim: Visser notes that money market fund assets rose again over three months, and says such cash build has historically occurred in panics rather than at stock highs; he reads it as cash flush from 4 to 5% yields rather than stress.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Large cash balances are a potential fuel source rather than a sign of trouble in his view.

insights.claim: Visser contends that rates rising hurts only weak balance sheets, since the government carries the debt, homeowners have positive equity, and housing sales are near lows, so higher rates act to weed out weak companies; AI-driven nominal GDP is what is pushing rates up.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Reframes higher yields as a symptom of AI-led growth and a selection mechanism.

insights.claim: Visser warns that the long end of the bond market rising and reaching for volatility in fixed income often means someone is being hurt; he says the place bears should watch is high-yield OAS, which has barely budged but is moving, alongside dollar strength.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Credit spread widening is the confirmation signal he wants before worrying about contagion.

themes.theme: Bear market inside a bull market

insights.claim: Visser's central thesis is a bear market within a bull market: Mag 7 and AI infrastructure names sit at all-time highs while rate-sensitive small caps, housing, autos, retail and restaurants trade at bear-market levels, and over 50% of S&P 500 market cap is in the technology side.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Index highs mask a deteriorating breadth that is structural rather than cyclical.

insights.claim: IWM relative to QQQ hit new lows on September 24th, the lowest since the iPhone era, and Visser says bad breadth accompanies Mag 7 leadership as it did when Amazon beat retailers, with the Russell 2000's roughly 4 trillion in combined value dwarfed by 30 trillion-dollar companies.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Small-cap relative weakness is persistent and not a signal of a market top.

insights.claim: Visser expects multiple compression even for large winners: AI lowers barriers to entry, speeds innovation cycles and shortens the durability of moats, so software like Salesforce could go from a 30 multiple to 10, while Micron already compressed; he says the S&P 500 PE was below 10 in 1980.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Argues the risk is de-rating of incumbents rather than a bubble in AI.

insights.claim: Visser states AI is not a bubble like the dot-com era, citing Nvidia at about 15 times next year's earnings versus Cisco at 100 PE, and says the market is pricing that AI competition destroys value beyond about five years.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Valuation for AI leaders is not extreme by his measure; the risk is elsewhere.

insights.claim: Visser's trade idea is to be long speed and short friction: short housing, private credit, and private equity names still trading down (naming Blue Owl as approaching lows), because disruption alpha comes on the short side of old businesses.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: A concrete short basket consistent with his rate and disruption view.

insights.claim: Visser suggests Visa and Mastercard face pressure and multiple compression because agents have no attachment to cards, brands or subscriptions and will use crypto and stablecoins, though he says Visa was the name brought up to him most often.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Payment incumbents are a possible short if agentic payments migrate to stablecoins.

themes.theme: Consumer agents as the next AI moment

insights.claim: Visser says consumer agents are the driver of the market now and the next 12 months, citing Meta's Muse launch with partners such as PayPal, Expedia, Shopify and Instacart, and Meta stock up 14% on Monday, lifting Intel, AMD and other Mag 7 names.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Consumer agent adoption is an explicit catalyst for compute and infrastructure demand.

insights.claim: Visser interprets Meta's rapid model releases (1.1, 1.2, 1.3 each about three weeks apart, then the consumer launch), after Zuckerberg said in July that AI development had not accelerated as expected, as evidence of recursive self-improvement arriving, in line with his reading of Leopold Aschenbrenner's 2027 timing.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Pace of capability improvement is being underestimated even by insiders.

insights.claim: Visser expects consumer agent token usage to explode based on download surges, and says enterprise agents came in the first half of 2026 while consumer agents are just starting, making infrastructure and compute needs insatiable.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Token demand growth supports the infrastructure basket.

insights.claim: Visser says his agentic infrastructure thematic portfolio is up 46% against 10% for the Mag 7 and that Salesforce is down 10% year-to-date; he expects infrastructure compute names to outperform hyperscalers and SaaS, which will face competition from each other, OpenAI and Anthropic.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Preference for picks-and-shovels over platforms with pricing pressure.

insights.claim: Visser expects the consumer-agent hype to favor biology and drug discovery more than consumer revenue, citing a reported Claude-discovered enzyme system similar to CRISPR, Silico Medicine and McKinsey's work on accelerated drug discovery cycles.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Healthcare and pharma could join the agentic theme as a research-driven story.

insights.claim: Visser cites Blackstone's John Gray describing 21% higher AI spending at portfolio companies over a year with returns already appearing in productivity, margins and earnings, and says the limiting factor is now the physical world.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Evidence AI spend is earning returns supports the physical infrastructure investment case.

insights.claim: Visser argues tokenization plus AI agents will increase the velocity of money and expand M2 as wealth becomes transactable, and that public equities will be broken up into more tokenized asset classes, which he calls the most important thing happening.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Structural shift in asset ownership and monetary aggregates that older backtests ignore.

insights.claim: Visser's ghost rails thesis is that crypto rails were built for 15 to 16 years awaiting an app-store moment, and that AI agents (which have no attachment to Visa or cards) rather than humans will use stablecoins and programmable money, like the iPhone app store followed the internet build-out.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Frames agents as the demand catalyst for crypto adoption, not retail humans.
insights.quote: The AI agents are the app store

insights.claim: Visser calls crypto a Peter Lynch-style early-stage bull market, and says he has been moving money from smaller agentic positions into crypto.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Shows his portfolio rotation toward crypto and tokenization exposure.

insights.claim: Visser's 46-name tokenized crypto index is up 31% for the month versus Bitcoin up 6.5%, with 44 of 46 names above the 50-day average; he says Bitcoin is not what to watch and that crypto rose despite rising rates.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Breadth in crypto is strong even though Bitcoin lags, and rates have not hurt it.

insights.claim: Visser says this week brought agent-payments news: BlackRock's paper on the machine-native economy and moving model portfolios on-chain via Ondo Finance, NYSE teaming with blockchain.com on tokenization, Robinhood teasing stock tokens, Coinbase trading on Muse, and Stripe as part of the agentic payments picture.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Institutional tokenization and agentic payment rails are progressing quickly.

insights.claim: Visser cites an a16z paper (May) claiming AI dramatically lowers barriers to using programmable money and that agents could aggressively disintermediate existing payment and subscription models.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Supports the agents-drive-crypto thesis from a well-known crypto venture firm.

themes.theme: Age, adoption and the time mismatch

insights.claim: Visser argues bearish macro commentators are mostly over 50 and few use AI, citing that only 2.2% of the 55 to 64 age bracket use AI, so their linear backtests miss the new regime; he calls this future shock and a time mismatch.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Explains persistent bearish consensus and suggests information advantage for AI-native investors.

insights.claim: Visser says entrepreneurship is booming because AI lets companies start without capital or debt, so rates do not hurt new businesses, and house prices will fall in about five years once building costs drop.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Points to disinflation and new business formation not sensitive to rates.

insights.claim: Visser notes the Hugging Face agent-swarm incident with an OpenAI researcher's takeaway that people underestimated AI, and says people are consistently underestimating AI progress, as Zuckerberg did.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Underestimation risk supports his bullish infrastructure stance.

insights.claim: Visser says AI stocks 'dropping 10% on Monday' warnings are noise, comparing them to the pause trade knee-jerk that marked the low, and calls the infrastructure trade well positioned with the best week since then.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, host
insights.so_what: Contrarian to AI-bubble fear headlines; dips have been bought.
